title: What are the common microservices anti-patterns and their fixes — over-splitting (start with a modular monolith), chatty services (BFF/aggregation), the "god gateway" (keep business logic out of the gateway), retry storms/thundering herd (backoff + jitter + circuit breaker + retry budgets), tight coupling via shared libraries (share contracts, not code), and no service ownership?
shortTitle: What are the common microservices anti-patterns and their fixes?

s1_definition.profdef: Microservices anti-patterns are recurring mistakes that reintroduce the problems microservices are meant to solve. The common ones are over-splitting (creating too many tiny services before boundaries are understood), chatty services (one request triggering many fine-grained network calls), the god gateway (stuffing business logic into the API gateway), retry storms and thundering herd (naive retries amplifying an outage), tight coupling via shared libraries (shared domain code forcing lockstep deploys), and no service ownership (no team accountable for a service). The fixes are, respectively: start with a modular monolith and extract services only when needed; use a Backend-for-Frontend or aggregation layer to reduce round trips; keep the gateway limited to cross-cutting concerns; apply exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, and retry budgets; share contracts rather than code; and assign clear single-team ownership to every service.
s1_definition.analogy: When National Bank of India modernizes, it can trip over the same mistakes repeatedly. Over-splitting is like giving every single clerk their own separate office building for a task two people could share — now they spend all day couriering memos between buildings. Chatty services is the loan desk phoning five other desks for one application instead of getting a single combined report. A god gateway is the front-door security guard who, instead of just checking IDs, also tries to approve loans himself — overloaded and blocking everyone. Retry storms are a hundred anxious customers all redialing the same busy number at the exact same second, keeping it permanently jammed. Tight coupling via shared libraries is every department forced to re-issue its entire rulebook the day one rule changes. No service ownership is a department that everyone uses but no one is responsible for, so when it breaks nobody fixes it. Each has a known, practical fix.
s1_definition.oneliner: The common microservices anti-patterns — over-splitting, chatty services, god gateway, retry storms, shared-library coupling, and no ownership — each reintroduce the pain microservices should remove, and each has a standard fix you should apply deliberately.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Microservices anti-patterns are recurring mistakes that reintroduce the problems microservices are meant to solve. The common ones are over-splitting (creating too many tiny services before boundaries are understood), chatty services (one request triggering many fine-grained network calls), the god gateway (stuffing business logic into the API gateway), retry storms and thundering herd (naive retries amplifying an outage), tight coupling via shared libraries (shared domain code forcing lockstep deploys), and no service ownership (no team accountable for a service). The fixes are, respectively: start with a modular monolith and extract services only when needed; use a Backend-for-Frontend or aggregation layer to reduce round trips; keep the gateway limited to cross-cutting concerns; apply exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, and retry budgets; share contracts rather than code; and assign clear single-team ownership to every service.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When National Bank of India modernizes, it can trip over the same mistakes repeatedly. Over-splitting is like giving every single clerk their own separate office building for a task two people could share — now they spend all day couriering memos between buildings. Chatty services is the loan desk phoning five other desks for one application instead of getting a single combined report. A god gateway is the front-door security guard who, instead of just checking IDs, also tries to approve loans himself — overloaded and blocking everyone. Retry storms are a hundred anxious customers all redialing the same busy number at the exact same second, keeping it permanently jammed. Tight coupling via shared libraries is every department forced to re-issue its entire rulebook the day one rule changes. No service ownership is a department that everyone uses but no one is responsible for, so when it breaks nobody fixes it. Each has a known, practical fix.

**One line to remember:** The common microservices anti-patterns — over-splitting, chatty services, god gateway, retry storms, shared-library coupling, and no ownership — each reintroduce the pain microservices should remove, and each has a standard fix you should apply deliberately.

sections.s2_technical:
Over-splitting is creating many tiny services before you understand the domain boundaries. Each service adds network calls, deployment pipelines, monitoring, and distributed-debugging cost, so splitting too early multiplies overhead for features that a single module could have handled. The symptom is a feature that two engineers could build becoming six services with constant cross-service coordination. The fix is to start with a modular monolith — one deployable with strong internal module boundaries — and extract a module into its own service only when there is a concrete need, such as independent scaling or a separate team owning it. You let real pressure, not fashion, drive the split.

Chatty services is when serving one user request requires many fine-grained calls between services, for example a screen that calls the account service, then the card service, then the rewards service, then the offers service, each a separate network round trip. Network calls are far slower than in-process calls, so latency balloons and the failure surface grows. The fix is a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) or aggregation layer that makes one call from the client and fans out to the services server-side, often in parallel, combining the results into a single response. This cuts client round trips and lets you optimize the fan-out. A small example is a BFF endpoint `/dashboard` that calls account, card, and rewards concurrently and returns one combined payload.

The god gateway is putting business logic into the API gateway. The gateway should handle cross-cutting concerns — authentication, authorization, rate limiting, routing, TLS — but when teams start adding domain rules, transformations tied to business meaning, and orchestration into the gateway, it becomes a shared bottleneck that every team must coordinate to change and that fails catastrophically. The fix is to keep business logic out of the gateway and in the services, limiting the gateway to generic edge concerns, so it stays thin and independently stable.

Retry storms and thundering herd happen when a dependency slows or fails and all its callers retry aggressively at once. The retries pile load onto an already-struggling service, keeping it down (a self-inflicted denial of service), and when it briefly recovers, every caller hits it simultaneously (thundering herd) and knocks it over again. The fixes combine: exponential backoff so retries space out increasingly, jitter so callers do not retry in lockstep at the same instant, circuit breakers so callers stop hammering a failing dependency and fail fast, and retry budgets so the total retry rate is capped rather than unbounded. A small example is retrying after a randomized delay growing as base times two to the attempt, giving up after a few attempts, inside a circuit breaker.

Tight coupling via shared libraries is sharing domain code so that changing the library forces every consuming service to rebuild and redeploy, destroying independent deployment. The fix is to share contracts, not code: publish API schemas, event schemas, and thin generated clients, but keep business logic inside each service. Some genuinely generic utility code is acceptable, but shared domain models and business rules are the trap.

No service ownership is when a service has no single accountable team, so no one maintains it, responds to its incidents, or evolves it, and it rots. The fix is clear ownership: every service is owned by exactly one team responsible for its development, on-call, SLAs, and roadmap, often formalized with a service catalog and "you build it, you run it" accountability.

The senior framing that ties these together is that microservices are an organizational and operational commitment, not just a technical one. Most of these anti-patterns come from adopting microservices prematurely or partially — splitting before boundaries are clear, or splitting the code without splitting the ownership and the resilience. The disciplined approach is to start simple (modular monolith), split along real business boundaries only when a real need arises, keep the edge thin, make every remote call resilient, share contracts not code, and give every service an accountable owner. A further nuance is that observability (distributed tracing, per-service metrics) is what lets you detect chatty paths and retry storms early, so investing in it is part of avoiding these anti-patterns.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's platform exhibits several of these anti-patterns and the team fixes them one by one.

Problem 1 — Chatty dashboard. The mobile dashboard made four separate calls to account, card, rewards, and offers services, and on slow networks it felt sluggish and sometimes partially failed. This is the chatty-services anti-pattern; the fix is a BFF that aggregates the four calls into one.

Problem 2 — Retry storm. When the rewards service slowed, every dashboard request retried immediately and repeatedly, overwhelming rewards and keeping it down. This is the retry-storm and thundering-herd anti-pattern; the fix is backoff with jitter plus a circuit breaker and a retry budget.

Problem 3 — God gateway creep. Someone started adding reward-calculation logic into the API gateway. This is the god-gateway anti-pattern; the fix is to keep that logic in the rewards service and leave the gateway thin.

We will model a BFF that aggregates downstream calls concurrently, a resilient caller using backoff-with-jitter, a circuit breaker, and a retry budget, demonstrating the chatty-to-aggregated fix and the retry-storm fix.

The code will have downstream services, a `DashboardBff` that aggregates concurrently, a `ResilientCaller` with backoff, jitter, circuit breaker, and a retry budget, and a demo that aggregates a dashboard in one call and shows the resilient caller surviving a failing dependency without a retry storm.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a dashboard request for Rajesh needing account, card, and rewards data; rewards is failing.

Step 1 — Instead of the client making three separate calls (the chatty anti-pattern), it makes one call to the BFF. The BFF fans out to account, card, and rewards concurrently on server-side threads.

Step 2 — Account and card return ok; rewards fails. The BFF handles the failure gracefully, marking rewards unavailable, and combines the three results into one response. The client got a single fast call with partial data rather than three round trips and a hard failure.

Step 3 — Separately, the resilient caller invokes the failing rewards service. On the first failure it does not immediately hammer again; it waits an exponentially growing delay with random jitter, so many callers would not retry in lockstep — this prevents the thundering herd.

Step 4 — The caller retries up to its maximum attempts, consuming from its retry budget. Because the budget caps total retries, a widespread outage cannot produce unbounded retry load that amplifies the failure.

Step 5 — The circuit breaker counts failures, and after three it opens, so subsequent calls fail fast with a fallback instead of waiting and retrying at all. This stops the self-inflicted denial of service that a retry storm would cause and lets the struggling rewards service recover.

Step 6 — Together the BFF fixes the chatty pattern and the resilient caller fixes the retry storm, while keeping all the business logic in the services and out of the gateway.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The common microservices anti-patterns each reintroduce the very pain microservices are meant to remove, and I know the standard fix for each. Over-splitting is creating too many tiny services before the domain boundaries are understood, so a feature two engineers could build becomes six services with constant coordination; the fix is to start with a modular monolith and extract a service only when a real need like independent scaling or separate team ownership appears, letting pressure rather than fashion drive the split.

Chatty services is one user request triggering many fine-grained network calls, which balloons latency and failure surface because network calls are far slower than in-process ones; the fix is a Backend-for-Frontend or aggregation layer that takes one client call and fans out to the services concurrently server-side, returning a single combined response. The god gateway is stuffing business logic into the API gateway until it becomes a shared bottleneck everyone must coordinate to change; the fix is to keep the gateway limited to cross-cutting edge concerns like authentication, rate limiting, routing, and TLS, and keep all domain logic in the services.

Retry storms and thundering herd happen when a struggling dependency's callers all retry aggressively and in lockstep, amplifying the outage and re-killing the service the moment it recovers; the fix combines exponential backoff so retries space out, jitter so callers do not retry at the same instant, circuit breakers so callers stop hammering a failing dependency and fail fast, and retry budgets so total retry load is capped. Tight coupling via shared libraries is sharing domain code so a library change forces every service to rebuild and redeploy; the fix is to share contracts, not code, publishing API and event schemas and thin clients while keeping business logic inside each service. No service ownership is a service with no accountable team, so it rots; the fix is clear single-team ownership with on-call and SLAs, often formalized in a service catalog under you-build-it-you-run-it.

In my banking platform I fixed a chatty mobile dashboard with a BFF that aggregated account, card, and rewards into one call, and I fixed a rewards-service retry storm with backoff, jitter, a circuit breaker, and a retry budget so a slow rewards service no longer collapsed the dashboard path, all while keeping the reward logic in the service and out of the gateway.

The framing I always end on is that microservices are an organizational and operational commitment, not just a technical one, and most of these anti-patterns come from adopting them prematurely or partially. The disciplined approach is to start simple, split along real business boundaries only when there is a genuine need, keep the edge thin, make every remote call resilient, share contracts not code, give every service an accountable owner, and invest in observability so chatty paths and retry storms are caught early.

The one-line summary I give is: the microservices anti-patterns are over-splitting, chatty services, the god gateway, retry storms, shared-library coupling, and no ownership, and the fixes are start as a modular monolith, aggregate with a BFF, keep the gateway thin, use backoff with jitter plus circuit breakers and retry budgets, share contracts not code, and assign one accountable team per service.
